messages.body_plain:
Hi GenPing,

It does sound like it is something going wrong with elevatr - perhaps try somethings just with that package and see if that's where the issue lies. E.g.

library(elevatr)
library(sp)
library(raster)
lat <- -35
long <- 145
resolution <- 30
zmin <- 0
xdims <- 200
ydims <- 200
xy <- data.frame(x = long, y = lat)
coordinates(xy)  <- ~x + y
proj4string(xy)  <- "+init=epsg:4326"
xy <- as.data.frame(spTransform(xy, CRS("+init=epsg:3395")))
e <- extent(c(xy$x - floor(xdims/2) * resolution, xy$x +
                ceiling(xdims/2) * resolution, xy$y - floor(ydims/2) *
                resolution, xy$y + ceiling(ydims/2) * resolution))
r <- raster(e)
res(r) <- resolution
crs(r) <- "+init=epsg:3395"
z  <- ceiling(log((cos(lat * pi/180) * 2 * pi * 6378137)/(256 * resolution), 2))
z <- ifelse(z > 14, 14, z)
r2 <- get_elev_raster(r, z = z, src = "aws")
plot(r2)

All the best,
Mike

messages.subject: shade effect
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
I'm computing microclimate conditions with nichemapR.

1) I am confused with the TAREF variable. If I understand TAREF is equal to the temperature input representative of mesoclimate. So TAREF has to account for coarse topography but not for vegetation. I computed microclimate at 1.5m above the ground whith minshade=0 and maxshade=90 (REFhyt was fixed to 2m). I get low difference between TALOC without and with shading effect. Moreover, the difference between TALOC and TAREF is also low whatever the shading level. May be I do something wrong but it's like TAREF is not corrected for shading at REFhyt before to be used to compute TALOC at USRhyt. Any ideas?

2)If I understand correctly the model, the effect of vegetation can be taken into account  through two ways: a) by feeding minshade and maxshade and b) by using adapted wind profile to the vegetation obvserved in the landscape. does another way exist?

3) I have recently tested several mesoclimate input (ERA5, E-obs, ...), and it seems that microclimate predictions are highly sensitive and correlated to the quality of mesoclimate data. For instance, microclimate predictions using E-obs data underestimate by 2°C in average microclimate temperatures, while when they are computed from ERA5 data, underestimation increase with elevation in Pyrenees. Does anyone know the best way to correct for this bias ? Another thing that disturbed me: microclimate predictions have lower predictive performance that a simple bilinear downscalling using CHELSA data... I don't know what I am doing wrong but I spent a lot of time to tune the model (soil moisture model, LAI, vegetation phenology) and I don't understand why I don't get better results.

Thanks by advance for your help.
All the best,
Romain

messages.subject: Re: shade effect
messages.body_plain:
Hi Romain,

1) TAREF is indeed representative of the mesoclimate, measured high enough from the ground that there are no microclimatic influences. There is an assumed vertical profile of change in air temperature with height such that, yes, there won't be much difference initially, but as you get down to a few cms above the ground, there will be big effects for a small change in local height. So you're not doing anything wrong - it's just the assumed physical relationship.

2) Yes you can capture (roughly) the effect of a forest canopy using horizon angles, such that there is no direct solar unless the sun is above the horizon angle and the effects of the diffuse radiation and sky temperature are also constrained by the resulting portion of the hemisphere that is sky, the rest of the hemisphere being assumed to be radiating at the reference air temperature. I've done this before, in addition to cutting down the wind speed, to get a reasonably good estimate of conditions in a forest. Also, check out microclimc <https://github.com/ilyamaclean/microclimc> which has sophisticated tools for under-canopy calculations of microclimate that can be used in conjunction with the NicheMapR microclimate model.

3) Your microclimate predictions will of course be strongly affected by the accuracy of the forcing data. You can add an offset to the air temps with the 'warm' input parameter if you are able to quantify the bias. Re the predictive performance issue - yes statistical models will often outperform physical models from a predictive point of view when interpolating a single variable, but the power of the physical models is that their generality. Statistical models often get it wrong when you extrapolate them.

Hope that helps,
Mike

messages.subject: Spectral reflectance curve and the REFL parameter
messages.subject_clean: Spectral reflectance curve and the REFL parameter
messages.body_plain:
Dear Mike,

I'm predicting intertidal mussel body temperatures using microclimate().

Gehman & Harley (2019; https://doi.org/10.1002/ecs2.2683) have estimated the spectral reflectance curve (between 300 and 1100 nm) of the shells of two types of mussels (see Fig 4A in their paper).

How can I integrate it in NicheMapR? Can the REFL parameter take multiple values to take into account varying reflectances over a range of wavelengths?

Thanks for your help!

Best,

Jonathan

messages.subject: Re: Spectral reflectance curve and the REFL parameter
messages.subject_clean: Spectral reflectance curve and the REFL parameter
messages.body_plain:
Dear Jonathan,

The REFL parameter is the 'reflectivity' of an object, specifically for the solar spectrum. A reflectance curve tells you how energy is absorbed across different wavelengths. If you know the intensity of energy across different wavelengths for incoming radiation then you can use that to get an appropriately weighted mean reflectivity of the object. As you would have seen in that paper you referred to, "The absorption spectrum (350–1100 nm) was multiplied by the power spectrum of incoming solar radiation measured at the Hopkins Marine Station (data courtesy of M. Denny; see Denny and Harley 2006 <https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/ecs2.2683#ecs22683-bib-0010> for details). The resulting energy absorbed is expressed in Wm−2." The reported the total energy absorbed but if they divided that by the total incoming energy and converted to a percentage, they would have the REFL parameter required by the model.

All the best,
Mike

messages.subject: Re: Spectral reflectance curve and the REFL parameter
messages.subject_clean: Spectral reflectance curve and the REFL parameter
messages.body_plain:
Thank you for the clarifications Mike!

So, I can either use their estimations of absorbed energy and the total irradiance (using ASTM G-173 standard irradiance spectrum) within their range of wavelengths (code chunk 1 below) or calculate it directly from spectral reflectance curves (code chunk 2). Correct?
### 1. calculation of REFL using absorbed energy (W/m2) calculated within 350-1100 nm for two types of mussels (eroded vs uneroded):

astmg173 <- read.csv(file.path(path, "astmg173.csv"), header=T) # ASTM G-173 standard irradiance spectrum for dry air derived from SMARTS v. 2.9.2 (https://doi.org/10.1016/S0038-092X(01)00054-8)

absorbed_uneroded <- 589.14
absorbed_eroded <- 532.98

minWL <- 350
maxWL <- 1100

totalsolarenergy_WL <- sum(astmg173[which(astmg173[,"Wvlgth.nm"]>=minWL & astmg173[,"Wvlgth.nm"]<=maxWL),"Direct.circumsolar.W.m.2.nm.1"]) # solar irradiance within the specified range of wavelengths

REFL_uneroded <- 1-(absorbed_uneroded/totalsolarenergy_WL) # =0.1879011
REFL_eroded <- 1-(absorbed_eroded/totalsolarenergy_WL) # =0.2653147

### 2. calculation of REFL using reflectance spectra within 350-1100 nm:

reflectance_uneroded # reflectance values (0-1) extracted from Fig 4A
reflectance_eroded # reflectance values (0-1) extracted from Fig 4A
solarirradiance # ASTM G-173 direct solar irradiance (W/m2/nm) at the wavelengths that match those of reflectance_uneroded  and reflectance_eroded

REFL_uneroded <- sum(reflectance_uneroded*solarirradiance)/sum(solarirradiance) # =0.1611066
REFL_eroded <- sum(reflectance_eroded*solarirradiance)/sum(solarirradiance) # =0.2459432

I guess the small difference in reflectivity values between both methods is due to the fact that the authors used the solar irradiance spectrum measured at their location. I would rather go for the second method so I don't mix different sources of irradiance data. What do you think?

Thanks again for your help!

Best,

Jonathan

messages.subject: Re: Spectral reflectance curve and the REFL parameter
messages.subject_clean: Spectral reflectance curve and the REFL parameter
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jonathan,

That looks good. The difference between methods would indeed be affected by the different irradiance spectra used but it could also be due to differences in the wavelength bands between the observed and predicted values, so that when you sum the energy across a given range you've got different accuracies of integration. You could use R's approxfun method to generate a spline function of the observed solar irradiance vs. wavelength and then use that to get the predicted irradiances at exactly those wavelengths for which you have data. Also, as Warren Porter pointed out, there is a lot of energy in the 1100 to 2600 nm region and you're implicitly assuming that what happens out in that range is similar to what happens in the 350-1100 range.

All the best,
Mike

messages.body_plain:
Hi Mike,

Great thanks! Yes I know there is a lot of energy beyond 1100 nm but unfortunately we won’t have the possibility to make those measurements… So I’ll have to stick with the data from Gehman & Harley (2019) and discuss the point. I calculated that 18.27% of the solar irradiance is not accounted for when having data within 350-1100 nm.

Regarding the interpolation of data, I already used smooth.spline() to smooth reflectance data (previously digitized with WebPlotDigitizer) so that they match the wavelengths in the ASTM G-173 irradiance dataset (i.e., every 0.5 nm between 350-400 nm and every 1 nm beyond). Do you suggest I try to get an even finer resolution? Here is the full code and the data if you want to have a look.
path <- "YOURPATH"

astmg173 <- read.csv(file.path(path, "astmg173.csv"), header=T) # ASTM G-173 standard irradiance spectrum for dry air derived from SMARTS v. 2.9.2 (https://doi.org/10.1016/S0038-092X(01)00054-8)

minWL <- 350
maxWL <- 1100

totalsolarenergy_inf <- sum(astmg173[,"Direct.circumsolar.W.m.2.nm.1"]) # total solar irradiance
totalsolarenergy_WL <- sum(astmg173[which(astmg173[,"Wvlgth.nm"]>=minWL & astmg173[,"Wvlgth.nm"]<=maxWL),"Direct.circumsolar.W.m.2.nm.1"]) # solar irradiance within the specified range of wavelengths
solarenergyleft <- 1-(totalsolarenergy_WL/totalsolarenergy_inf) # proportion of the total solar irradiance not accounted for

uneroded <- read.csv(file.path(path, "Gehman&Harley2019Fig4A_Uneroded.csv"), header=F)
eroded <- read.csv(file.path(path, "Gehman&Harley2019Fig4A_Eroded.csv"), header=F)
colnames(uneroded) <- c("wavelength", "reflectivity")
colnames(eroded) <- c("wavelength", "reflectivity")

plot(uneroded$wavelength, uneroded$reflectivity, ylim=c(0, 0.7), xlim=c(300, 1200), pch=19, col="black")
points(eroded$wavelength, eroded$reflectivity, pch=19, col="grey")

xl <- astmg173[which(astmg173[,"Wvlgth.nm"]>=minWL & astmg173[,"Wvlgth.nm"]<=maxWL), "Wvlgth.nm"]

mussel_reflectance <- data.frame(wavelength=xl, eroded=NA, uneroded=NA)

dta <- uneroded

sp <- smooth.spline(dta$wavelength, dta$reflectivity)
sp.pred <- data.frame(x=xl, y=predict(sp, xl)[["y"]])
lines(sp.pred$x, sp.pred$y, col="red")

mussel_reflectance$uneroded <- sp.pred$y

dta <- eroded

sp <- smooth.spline(dta$wavelength, dta$reflectivity)
sp.pred <- data.frame(x=xl, y=predict(sp, xl)[["y"]])
lines(sp.pred$x, sp.pred$y, col="red")

mussel_reflectance$eroded <- sp.pred$y

mussel_reflectance <- cbind(mussel_reflectance, data.frame(solar=astmg173[match(mussel_reflectance$wavelength, astmg173[,"Wvlgth.nm"]),"Direct.circumsolar.W.m.2.nm.1"]))

solarirradiance <- mussel_reflectance$solar

REFL_uneroded <- sum(mussel_reflectance$uneroded*solarirradiance)/sum(solarirradiance)
REFL_eroded <- sum(mussel_reflectance$eroded*solarirradiance)/sum(solarirradiance)

REFL_uneroded # =0.1611066
REFL_eroded # =0.2459432

Best,

Jonathan
​
